posts.title: France Raises 2026 Wine Harvest Forecast To 34.9 Million hl
posts.excerpt: France has raised its wine-production estimate, but the revised forecast remains below last year and the five-year average.
posts.meta_title: France's 2026 Wine Harvest Forecast Revised | BevOry
posts.meta_description: France raises its 2026 wine forecast to 34.9 million hl, still below recent averages. Read the regional context and what it means for buyers.
posts.selection_note: A 7 October update to a major wine-producing country's harvest outlook, with clear figures and a useful distinction between volume and bottle quality.
posts.content:
France's agriculture ministry has raised its 2026 wine-production forecast to 34.9 million hectolitres, from 33.9 million in September. The update was released on 7 October, according to Reuters' report.

A Bigger Forecast, Still A Small Harvest

The revised total remains 2% below 2025 and 14% below the 2021-2025 average. Better-than-expected yields in Languedoc-Roussillon drove the upgrade. Across France, reduced vineyard area, drought and intense summer heat have weighed on production.

A national total can conceal very different regional harvests.

Volume Is Not A Tasting Score

Our reading of these figures is straightforward: they describe supply, not how every French wine will taste. A smaller harvest alone cannot tell you that a particular bottle is better, worse or worth more.

WSET's explanation of vintage variation shows why local conditions matter. Weather affects grape health and ripeness, and even nearby vineyards can face different hazards. Producer decisions also shape the finished wine.

What Indian Wine Buyers Can Use

A harvest forecast is useful background for following French wine. It is not a reason, on its own, to rush a purchase or assume an Indian retail price will rise.

For a bottle you are considering, compare the producer, wine name, region, vintage and pack size. On BevOry, select your city before comparing listings. A Bordeaux vintage and a Champagne house blend deserve their own questions; neither is fully explained by France's headline production number.

posts.title: What Does Vintage Mean On Wine? A Buying Guide For India
posts.excerpt: The year on a wine label refers to the grape harvest, not the bottling date. Here is how to use it without assuming older means better.
posts.meta_title: Wine Vintage Meaning & Buying Guide India | BevOry
posts.meta_description: Learn what a wine vintage means, how NV Champagne differs and why older is not always better. Compare exact bottles and city prices on BevOry.
posts.selection_note: A practical label-reading question connected to current harvest news; focuses on decisions a shopper can make rather than a universal vintage ranking.
posts.content:
A wine's vintage is the year its grapes were harvested. A bottle marked 2023 identifies a harvest year, not necessarily the year it was bottled or bought. The number is useful, but it is not a quality score.

WSET's wine-label guide explains the two questions vintage helps answer: how old a wine is, and what that growing season was like.

Why The Same Wine Can Change From Year To Year

A cooler or wetter season can ripen grapes differently from a warm, dry one. Frost, hail and drought can also affect a vineyard. Bordeaux, for example, has considerable year-to-year weather variation.

The WSET vintage explainer describes how some producers embrace those differences, while larger blends may aim for consistency. The useful comparison is the same producer and wine across years, not every bottle carrying the same date.

Is An Older Vintage Better?

Not automatically. Some wines gain interesting flavours with bottle age, but most are intended to be enjoyed young and fresh. Keeping an everyday wine longer does not turn it into a collector's bottle.

For dinner this weekend, ask about the wine's style and recommended drinking window. A year printed in large type gives you less information than that answer. For a special bottle, the producer's guidance and storage history deserve attention before the age attracts a premium.

What Does NV Mean On Champagne?

NV means non-vintage. These wines blend more than one harvest year, helping the producer keep a recognisable house style. Vintage Champagne expresses one harvest year instead. WSET's sparkling-wine guide explains the distinction.

A missing year on a non-vintage bottle is therefore not a missing quality credential. Buy it for the style you enjoy, rather than treating NV as a warning.

Storage Matters More Than A Birthday

For long-term ageing, WSET recommends a steady 10-15 degrees C and protection from bright light. Its storage guidance cautions against kitchens with large temperature swings.

In an Indian home, a cupboard beside the stove is a poor place to build a wine collection. Before paying more for an older bottle, ask where it has been kept. A date cannot repair heat damage.

Comparing Wine Prices In Mumbai, Delhi Or Bengaluru

Match the producer, wine name, vintage and bottle size before comparing prices. Two different years can be two different buying decisions, even when the front labels look almost identical. Select the relevant city on BevOry and compare the exact listing, rather than treating a national price headline as your local price.

posts.title: Champagne vs Prosecco: Taste, Indian Pairings And Buying
posts.excerpt: Compare Champagne's bottle fermentation with Prosecco's usual tank method, decode Brut and Extra Dry, and choose a style for Indian dishes.
posts.meta_title: Champagne vs Prosecco: India Buying Guide | BevOry
posts.meta_description: Compare Champagne and Prosecco by grapes, bubbles and sweetness. Find Indian food pairings, serving tips and city prices on BevOry.
posts.selection_note: A clear style comparison that answers method, sweetness and meal-pairing questions; city-price advice avoids unverified MRPs or availability promises.
posts.content:
Champagne is a sparkling wine from Champagne in France; Prosecco is a Glera-led Italian wine, usually made sparkling by the tank method. They offer different styles, rather than two grades of the same drink. The useful choice begins with flavour, sweetness and the meal.

Where They Come From, And Which Grapes Matter

Comite Champagne identifies Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier as the region's most-used grapes. A white Champagne can include dark-skinned grapes; the wine's colour does not tell you its entire blend.

Prosecco DOC comes from north-eastern Italy, in Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Its principal grape is Glera. The Prosecco DOC consortium's Glera guide describes floral, pear, green-apple and citrus aromas associated with the variety.

Bottle Fermentation vs Tank Fermentation

Champagne's second fermentation takes place in the bottle. The wine then rests with the spent yeast, known as lees. Comite Champagne's maturation guide describes how yeast breakdown and slow oxidation develop the wine. Champagne must mature in the producer's cellars for at least 15 months before release; vintage cuvees require at least three years.

For the usual sparkling Prosecco DOC, the second fermentation happens in large pressure tanks, using the Martinotti, or Charmat, method. The consortium's winemaking explanation sets out that process. This is different from simply adding bubbles to a finished still wine.

What Changes In The Glass?

Lees ageing can bring brioche, toast and pastry notes to traditional-method wines. Tank-made styles usually emphasise fresh fruit and floral aromas. These are broad style clues, not a tasting note for every bottle. WSET's sparkling-wine guide explains how the methods influence flavour.

The same guide clears up an easy label trap: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Do not assume the words Extra Dry identify the driest wine on the shelf. Compare the sweetness designation as well as the name.

Indian Dishes To Put Alongside Them

For a fruit-led Brut Prosecco, try malai paneer tikka, lightly seasoned tandoori prawns or cucumber chaat with restrained chilli. A dry Champagne with toasty depth is worth trying with rava-fried fish, mushroom vol-au-vents or salted almonds.

These are pairing suggestions, not rules. Begin with milder portions of chutney and sauces, then taste the wine with the food. A rich sauce, strong chilli or sweet glaze can change the match more than the occasion on the calendar.

Serve Chilled, Not Frozen

Comite Champagne recommends 8-10 degrees C and a tulip-shaped glass with room for the aromas. Its serving guide suggests an ice-and-water bucket for chilling. For a fresh Prosecco, 8-10 degrees C is also a practical starting point; follow a producer's specific recommendation when available.

Keep the cork controlled and point the bottle away from people when opening. The aim is a clean pour, not a flying cork.

How To Compare Prices In India

Set Mumbai, Delhi, Gurgaon, Bengaluru or your own city on BevOry. Compare the exact producer, cuvee, Brut or Extra Dry designation, vintage or non-vintage style, and bottle size. A price for an entire category is less useful than the price of the bottle you plan to open.

Choose Prosecco when its fresh, fruit-led style suits your meal. Choose Champagne when you want the particular producer's blend and bottle-aged character. Neither needs to win every comparison.
